doors.programmer: You write Haro and, for the layer another language does best, you hand it a string of code and a list of data and take a list back. In the plan, a Python or JavaScript programmer will also write Haro in a syntax they know. Two different things: a syntax brings you, and a runtime brings your libraries.
doors.analyst: The statistical layer is R's, the machine-learning layer Python's, the logic layer Prolog's. You stay in one file and one list of results. The R door is in development and raises today, and the record says so.
doors.designer: There is nothing to design at the door itself. The record's lesson is its refusal: a language not on the list is refused by name, and "what about my language" has one answer.
doors.decision-maker: The door is the one place where the closure ends, by decision. At this commit its governance is designed and not yet built, and its way back, not yet closed, reaches host code. The vision's word "governed" is a design. Every call's duration is recorded in the trace today.
doors.educator: A learner sees which layer belongs to which language and runs a two-door pipeline. The lesson is the difference between reading a language, running it, and writing in its syntax.
doors.agent: You never reach the door by yourself. A function in an AI agent's file must carry a posture, and `external` fits a foreign runtime; and an AI model has no capability to produce effects (chapter 20).

doors.programmer: Your agent's mind is code you can test with ordinary promises. An AI model may serve as one faculty; it can never hold an effect.
doors.analyst: A fact or a rule you add makes the system know more, with no code change and no training, and every answer carries its why.
doors.designer: The system asks the user one accountable question at a time, and the question is handed to any door as a frame, so that a terminal, a page or an agent can render it. Only the terminal ran here.
doors.decision-maker: A decision costs nothing per call, runs offline and is the same tomorrow. The four agents still reserved are the next step.
doors.educator: The conversation asks and never answers first, and it uses a model's fluency only when a model is there, so a learner always sees the floor.
doors.agent: You may propose. You may not commit. A refusal names its law, and you can learn the platform from the platform and be corrected by it.

doors.programmer: A reply is a verdict you can test with ordinary promises: what was admitted, what was refused, and the state of the goal.
doors.analyst: The goal is the schema of a complete model. The gaps are the list of what is missing. The transcript and the checkpoints are the evidence of how each fact got in.

doors.decision-maker: A reply is judged before it counts. A refusal reaches a person with its context and a lifetime. The roster is honest: one agent of five is wired, and two of the five registers are not available.
doors.educator: The tutor is wise coding. It names the missing step as a question and never as the answer, in the learner's language, and its wording in three of those languages awaits a native reviewer.
doors.agent: You can drive the loop yourself with an answer source, and you must stop where you would have to invent. You cannot offer examples and be understood, and you are told by name when you ask for a reserved agent.

doors.programmer: A domain language model is a file you can read, diff and test: its facts, its laws and its goldens.
doors.analyst: A fact you add makes the model know more, and a law you add makes the graph refuse more, with no training; the model's own answers do not read it yet.
doors.designer: The model's refusal is part of its contract: the golden test says what it must decline to answer.
doors.decision-maker: The model can only say what the domain holds, and the gate keeps the record of what it refused and why.
doors.educator: Rung one is a model a learner can read in full. Rung two is small enough to train in front of a class.
doors.agent: What you propose is a fact the graph can admit or refuse, with a reason you can read.

doors.programmer: Your agent is a file and a few functions. It runs and believes it acted, and the disk does not move. You read the plan, choose the committing actor and the scope, and the court tells you in one sentence which rule refused you.
doors.analyst: Every proposal is a narrated plan of operations with the destructive steps flagged, and an audit line for each commit. You can read what the agent meant to do, step by step, without running it. The flags are by kind, not scored.
doors.designer: The plan is the one artefact that crosses from the agent to the person, and a person can reject one step. The Right to a Human says a person is reachable wherever a machine serves, and the right is held by judgment.
doors.decision-maker: You declare what each agent covers and how reversible it is before it may exist, and you decide the scope and the actor that commits. An AI model is structurally unable to commit, even when fooled; the threat model assumes it will be. The hardest part is the one the design leaves to you: which functions code allows an agent to call.
doors.educator: A learner's agent that tidies a course folder by deleting everything is a lesson in what a plan is. She sees what it would have done, and the files are still there.
doors.agent: You may rehearse without limit, inside the twin. Your only export is a plan, and you can be argued with over it. You may not commit. Today the argument is one-way: you do not yet receive the reviewer's objection and revise.

doors.programmer: You declare a world with braces, ask it to explain itself, and cross between worlds with a call that returns 0 and a `Why()` that names the gate. Watch the copy: configure, then register.
doors.analyst: You declare things, relations and a goal as a wanted state of the graph, and the gap is measured. Your truths and durations are narrated and not yet judged.
doors.designer: A world declares screens as intents, a refinement as a bounded knob, and where it appears. The shells generated today are stubs, and the persona a world serves is not a field.
doors.decision-maker: You declare who may cross where and at what risk, in three gates, and every cleared crossing leaves a decision: the block printed its rationale, and its record holds the authority and the risk of its moment. Your architect's file is text you own.
doors.educator: The record is thin. The education plan lists a ladder from practitioner to architect to contributor among five competing level schemes, and I say so. The exercise below is judged by running.
doors.agent: A world can be wrapped as an AI agent that the host ticks. A deploy by a language-model actor is refused, and nothing is deployed. The crossing between worlds is governed by the calling world's name and authority.
